B01:
RAG and fine-tuning solve different problems, and a 100,000-document customer-support knowledge base is where that difference starts costing money.

Use RAG when you need freshness and citations. It reads from the knowledge base at query time, so the answer reflects whatever the docs say this morning, and you can hand the user the exact source it came from.

Use fine-tuning when you need style and latency. Tone and the shape of a good answer go into the weights, so there's no retrieval hop on every request.

Now put those 100,000 documents back in the middle. If they change every week and your agents have to cite policy back to customers, retrieval wins, and it isn't close. If the corpus is stable and the real complaint is that answers sound off-brand or arrive slowly, tuning wins.

Plenty of teams end up doing both. What decides it is how often your content changes, how much a citation is worth to you, and how much latency your users will sit through.
B02:
One table. Twenty-three indexes. We dropped fourteen of them and write throughput doubled.

That client wasn't unusual, just further along a curve most teams are on. A query gets slow, someone adds an index, the query gets fast, and nobody comes back later to check whether the index is still earning its keep.

Meanwhile every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE has to maintain all of them. An index that has never served a single query still gets written on every row change, still eats disk, still has to be walked at vacuum time. You pay for it on every write, forever, and get nothing back.

Finding the fourteen took no hardware changes and no query rewrites. We pulled Postgres's own index-usage numbers and dropped everything that wasn't paying for itself.

Below: how to read those numbers, which indexes look dead but aren't, and how to drop one on a live table without taking the table down with it.
B03:
We hired 27 remote engineers last year. The first of them waited 12 days to merge a pull request. The last ones were merging on day 5.

Twelve days isn't a training problem. It's a queue. An access request sitting in someone else's inbox. Documentation that's easier to search than to trust. A new engineer with questions and no idea which channel to ask them in. None of it is dramatic on its own, and together it costs a week, which happens to be the week a new hire decides what kind of team they've joined.

The fixes were dull. We provisioned accounts before the start date instead of after it. We gave every new hire one named person they were allowed to interrupt. And we deleted more documentation than we wrote, because the stale pages were doing more damage than the missing ones.

Day 5 isn't a victory lap. It's what happens when the first week stops being a scavenger hunt. Here's the whole playbook, including the metrics we watch to keep it there.
B04:
We asked 412 designers how their design system is going. 61% said it's partially adopted at best.

That's the report in one line. The majority of these teams have a design system. Components exist. Documentation exists. And most of the product still isn't built out of them.

Adoption stalls for unglamorous reasons. Nobody owns the system, so nobody can say no to a one-off. The roadmap outruns the library, so a team ships its own button and moves on. Design and code drift until the Figma file and the repo describe two different products. Docs go stale, and a designer who gets burned by stale docs stops opening them.

The teams that get adoption right share a small set of habits, and those habits showed up consistently enough across industries, company sizes and maturity levels that we don't think it's noise.

The rest of the report breaks the numbers down and lays out what the high-adoption teams do differently.
B05:
It took me 14 months to build an emergency fund on a $52k salary.

The standard advice is 3 to 6 months of expenses, and it's right. A job loss, a medical bill, a surprise car repair: any one of them lands on a credit card if the cash isn't there. Simple advice. Miserable to execute.

The math was never the hard part. The number I could move into savings each month was small and it was obvious. What made it hard is that the balance moves slowly enough to look like it isn't moving. There's no compounding chart to admire and nothing to mention at a party.

What got me through was deciding once instead of every month. I automated the transfer so the money was gone before I could look at the balance and negotiate with myself.

Below is the specific version: what I cut, what I refused to cut, and what kept me going through the slow middle. If you've started and stalled, that middle part is the one to read.
B06:
Four days in Kyoto, and the best hour of it was before breakfast.

Fushimi Inari at 6am is worth the alarm. Walk up under the vermilion gates that early and the mountain path is almost entirely yours, which is not something anyone says about Fushimi Inari later in the day. Same gates, same photographs, a completely different walk.

We based ourselves in Gion. It's the geisha district, which makes it the obvious choice and the one that gets recommended to death. But the wooden machiya fronts and the lantern light do most of their work after dark, once the day crowds have thinned. An ordinary walk back to the room turns into the part of the day you remember.

Our last night was kaiseki: ¥18,000 a head. Not cheap, and I'd pay it again. Course after course of seasonal dishes, plated closer to art than to dinner.

B07:
The average mid-market company runs purchasing through 7 different tools: spreadsheets, email threads, ERP modules and standalone approval apps.

Seven systems means no system. A request is raised in one place and approved in another, so nobody can answer "where is it" without asking three people. Approvers don't know what's waiting on them, because their queue isn't anywhere in particular. Finance can't see committed spend until the invoice lands, which is the worst possible moment to find out.

That's how you get a 14-day approval cycle on a purchase nobody disagreed with. Companies that pull requests, approvals and vendor records into one workflow bring that down to 3 days.

Three days isn't a magic number. It's what's left once you delete the waiting.

The rest of this piece covers how purchasing tooling got this fragmented, what consolidation looks like day to day, and how to tell whether your process is bad enough to be worth changing.
B08:
On Tuesday an expired TLS certificate on an internal service took our platform down for four hours.

The service isn't one most of us think about. It sits in the request path, which is the part we'd stopped thinking about too. The certificate expired on schedule, exactly the way certificates do, and nothing was watching the date.

What turned an expiry into a four-hour outage was the failure mode. Alerts fired, but they fired all over the cascade, so the loudest ones were furthest from the cause. We spent a long time chasing errors on services that were fine.

Three things are changing:

- Automated certificate-expiry monitoring across all services, including internal ones.
- A documented rotation runbook for every internal certificate.
- Regular game-day testing of certificate failure modes, so the next one is a shape we've seen before.

The full timeline and the contributing factors are below. If you run internal services behind their own certificates, the second item is the cheap one and we should have done it years ago.

Vertical SaaS used to die on market size. The industry needed better software, the TAM couldn't return a fund, the partner passed. For twenty years that was the correct call.

AI changes the cost side of the arithmetic. When a small team can build, sell and support what used to take fifty people, the market doesn't have to be big. It has to be big enough for a small company, and far more markets clear that bar than cleared the old one.

Software for marinas: a $400M TAM. Most funds would have ignored it a decade ago. An AI-native team can serve that market profitably today, own the core workflow end to end, and grow into payments and insurance from there.

So here's the thesis. The next set of great vertical SaaS companies will be small teams in small markets, taking most of each one. If that's what you're building, write to us.

T01:
I sent thousands of cold emails last year and got an 8% reply rate. Five things did most of that work.

1/ Four lines. Who you are, why you're relevant to this person, what you want. Your prospect is scanning on a phone between meetings. Anything longer doesn't get more attention, it gets archived.

2/ One CTA. Not two, not a menu. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats every version that offers options, because each extra ask is one more decision the reader can put off until never.

3/ Personalize the first line, and only if it's real. "Loved your post on X" works when you read the post and can say something about it. Otherwise it reads exactly like the template it is.

4/ Follow up. Most of my replies came from email two or three, not email one. A polite bump isn't annoying, and silence isn't a no. It's usually a bad week.

5/ Track subject lines, send times and CTAs. The 8% came after I started running cold email as a system with a weekly iteration loop instead of a lottery ticket. Before that I was guessing and calling it outreach.
T02:
Most meetings should be memos.

Writing forces you to find out whether you have a point, and it leaves a record you can actually search. A meeting leaves nothing.

If an idea can't survive being written down, it won't survive a 60-minute meeting either.
T03:
19 months ago I put a $49 one-time product online. This week we crossed $10k MRR. No funding, no team.

1/ The first version was ugly. A $49 one-time purchase, no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales, which told me the one thing I needed to know: people would pay for this.

2/ The pivot came from customers, not from a plan. They kept coming back with the same recurring problem, and a one-time product couldn't serve it. In month 7 we moved to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks. Then it compounded.

3/ I onboarded every early customer myself, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote the roadmap for us. I still don't have a better source of product ideas.

4/ 19 months to $10k MRR is slow, and that's the honest headline. It's also 19 months that were profitable the whole way, which is why I'm still here to write this.

T05:
New paper on LLM-as-judge: 81% agreement with human evaluators across the board, 64% on creative tasks.

1/ 81% is high enough to be useful. On routine evaluation where an answer can be right or wrong, an LLM judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human rater, and it runs at a scale no panel of humans does.

2/ 64% on creative tasks is the finding that matters. Style, originality, taste: when there's no correct answer to converge on, judges and humans stop agreeing about what good even means.

3/ The likely reason is that judges reward what's easy to see. Structure, fluency, length. They like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ So use them for scale where the task has a right answer, and keep humans on the work where it doesn't. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.

R01: Automated code review promises lower defect rates and lighter reviewer workload, but existing tools are narrow in scope and imprecise. We present ReviewBot, which combines static analysis with learned models to report defects inside the pull-request workflow. We evaluated ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests drawn from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes. ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters at a 12% false-positive rate, which developers in our study rated acceptable for day-to-day use. The improvement is uneven, and where it concentrates is the more informative result: ReviewBot's largest gains are on cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns, the defect classes that traditional linters routinely miss. We also report what deployment at scale demands, including reviewer trust, control of alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines. On this evidence, automated review augments human reviewers rather than substituting for them. Adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning remain open problems, and we release our evaluation framework so that both can be tested against the same baseline.
R02:
We surveyed 156 enterprises about how they govern their data. The central finding is that 44% have no data-classification policy at all.

That one gap explains most of the others. An organization that cannot say which data is sensitive, regulated or business-critical cannot write access rules, retention schedules or encryption requirements that mean anything, and its incident response starts with a discovery exercise instead of a plan. Classification is not the mature end of data governance. It is the precondition for the rest of it.

Enterprises without that foundation report longer audit cycles and higher breach-response costs. AI programs surface the deficit faster, because they demand well-understood and well-labeled data before a single model is trained on it.

This whitepaper sets out a 5-step maturity model: discovery, then classification, then ownership, then policy enforcement, then continuous monitoring. Each step carries concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria, so a team can establish where it currently sits before deciding what to fix.

The number to act on is the 44%. Classification is unglamorous work, and everything downstream of it is gated on getting it done.
R03:
Contract review time is down 60% at firms piloting AI-assisted review. Work that consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, which moves the constraint from reading the contract to deciding what to do about it. For legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less, that is a hard number to argue with.

The failure mode is citations. These tools generate authorities that look entirely plausible and simply do not exist, and courts have shown little patience with filings that contain them. That risk does not shrink with volume, so every AI-assisted output still requires review by a qualified lawyer.

The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, built around competence, confidentiality and supervision. Read plainly, it permits the technology and leaves the output your responsibility.

For legal teams, the sequence that works is high-volume and lower-risk first, which is exactly what contract review is. Measure what you actually save rather than what you expect to. Keep a lawyer between the model and the client. The firms that pair the speed with the judgment will do the same work faster; the ones that skip the second half will explain themselves to a judge.
